idiom_name: IEnumerable<T>.Where / Select / OrderBy / Aggregate with deferred execution
implementation_notes: The standard query operators are the pattern: extension methods on IEnumerable<T> - Where for filter, Select for map, SelectMany for flat-map, OrderBy/Distinct for the positional stages, and Aggregate/Sum/Count for the terminal step - with ToList/ToDictionary/ToArray to materialise. Microsoft's documentation states that sequence-returning operators use deferred execution: the returned object 'stores all the information that is required to perform the action' and the query 'is not executed until the object is enumerated'. That replaces a foreach loop with an accumulator; keep the loop when the single pass mutates state or when the query must be stepped through element by element.
pitfalls: Deferred execution means the query re-runs on every enumeration: iterating the same IEnumerable twice repeats the work and any side effects, and a captured variable keeps its live value.

IQueryable<T> (EF Core and other providers) defers to the provider: only the translatable operator subset works, and a client-side method inside a lambda may throw or silently fall back to in-memory evaluation.
A query that is never enumerated never runs - a missing ToList/foreach turns an expected side effect into a no-op.

variants.name: LINQ query-expression (comprehension) syntax
variants.idiom_name: from ... where ... select / group by / join
variants.implementation_notes: The query-expression form is a comprehension surface over the same machinery: Microsoft's standard-query-operators page states that the query keywords are translated by the compiler into 'the equivalent method calls' and that the two forms are synonymous. Reach for it when the query is a join or a grouping (multiple from clauses are SelectMany, group ... by becomes GroupBy), and for the method chain when the pipeline is long and linear; the choice is local to the query, not to the codebase.
variants.code_sketch:
var perDept = from p in people
              where p.IsActive
              join d in departments on p.DeptId equals d.Id
              group p by d.Name into g
              select new { Dept = g.Key, Count = g.Count() };

foreach (var row in perDept)      // still deferred
    Console.WriteLine($"{row.Dept}: {row.Count}");
pitfalls: Not every operator has a query keyword (no keyword for Distinct, Take, Aggregate), so a comprehension usually has to be finished with method calls.
The translation is literal: an unsupported member or an ambiguous range variable surfaces as a compiler error inside the generated method call, not at the keyword.

variants.name: PLINQ (AsParallel over ParallelQuery<T>)
variants.implementation_notes: PLINQ implements the same query operators over ParallelQuery<T>: AsParallel() partitions the source across cores, the chain is otherwise written as usual, and AsOrdered()/AsSequential() restore ordering or fall back to sequential evaluation. Microsoft's PLINQ introduction describes it as 'a parallel implementation of the Language-Integrated Query (LINQ) pattern' with 'additional operators for parallel operations'. Use it only for large, CPU-bound, independent element functions - the same chain, a different execution policy.
variants.code_sketch:
var totals = orders
    .AsParallel()
    .Where(o => o.Total > 0)
    .GroupBy(o => o.Region)
    .Select(g => new { g.Key, Sum = g.Sum(o => o.Total) })
    .ToList();
pitfalls: Side effects and non-associative accumulation produce wrong results silently; deterministic order must be re-imposed with AsOrdered (which costs) or dropped deliberately.
Partitioning and merging have fixed overhead: for small sources PLINQ is slower than the sequential query, so measure before switching.
